title: JPMorgan vs. Citigroup: Which Stock Has the Edge After Q3 Results? - TradingView
content: Banking giants JPMorgan JPM and Citigroup C kicked off the third-quarter earnings season this week with contrasting results amid an uncertain economic backdrop. While JPMorgan reinforced its position as an industry leader in profitability and financial strength despite earnings miss, Citigroup delivered robust earnings growth as its multiyear restructuring efforts continued to gain momentum. Both banks benefited from stronger net interest income (NII), highlighting their resilience in an evolving operating environment. However, their investment propositions differ. JPMorgan's diversified business model, superior profitability, and solid balance sheet offer stability, while Citigroup's ongoing transformation, improving returns, and relatively attractive valuation could provide greater upside potential. With both banking giants demonstrating resilience, which stock presents the more compelling investment opportunity following their Q3 earnings results? Let us compare their financial performance, growth prospects, and valuations to determine which bank may offer investors the better opportunity. JPMorgan continues to benefit from its diversified business model, strong market position and consistent earnings-generating capabilities. Its leading consumer banking franchise, extensive credit card operations, investment banking and trading businesses, and expanding wealth management platform provide multiple revenue streams, helping it navigate changing economic conditions. A major growth driver for JPMorgan remains its strong deposit franchise and expanding loan portfolio. In the third quarter, NII increased 13% year over year to $27.1 billion, supported by higher deposit balances, growth in credit card lending and increased wholesale loan activity. Excluding Markets, NII rose 6% to $24.7 billion, indicating continued underlying banking momentum. Management projects 2026 NII of $106.2 billion. Its preliminary 2027 outlook calls for NII, excluding Markets, of $107 billion, supported by continued balance sheet expansion and higher interest rates. The Federal Reserve's 25-basis-point rate hike in September 2026 could provide an additional tailwind by supporting yields on floating-rate loans and interest-earning assets. However, higher deposit costs and the potential impact of elevated borrowing rates on loan demand could partially offset these benefits. Prudent risk management and a strong balance sheet further support its long-term prospects. As of Sept. 30, 2026, the company maintained a standardized common equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio of 13.9%, backed by $304 billion in CET1 capital. It also held $1.5 trillion in cash and marketable securities, providing substantial liquidity to navigate economic uncertainty and support business expansion. JPMorgan has a strong record of dividends and share repurchases, supported by its earnings strength and capital position. Over the past five years, the company has hiked its dividend six times and currently has a dividend yield of 1.9%. It also authorized a share repurchase program worth $50 billion. As of Sept. 30, 2026, JPMorgan had $48.94 billion remaining under its share repurchase authorization. JPMorgan Chase & Co. dividend-yield-ttm | JPMorgan Chase & Co. Quote Nevertheless, rising operating expenses remain concerning. Third-quarter expenses increased 12% year over year, outpacing revenue growth, reflecting higher compensation, technology spending and business expansion. Sustaining strong revenue momentum while maintaining expense discipline will be crucial for preserving its industry-leading profitability. Citigroup offers a different investment proposition, centered on improving profitability, operational efficiency and unlocking value through its ongoing strategic transformation. The bank's globally diversified businesses, particularly Services, Markets, Wealth and Institutional Banking, provide a solid foundation for long-term growth. Under CEO Jane Fraser, Citigroup has been working to simplify its organization. This includes exiting international consumer markets, streamlining operations, reducing management layers, cutting costs and focusing on higher-return businesses. The goal is to make C a leaner, more focused and profitable institution. Encouragingly, the transformation is beginning to deliver measurable improvements, with the company delivering positive operating leverage in the third quarter of 2026. Its efficiency ratio fell to 58.5% from 64.7% in the prior-year quarter, indicating improving profitability. NII, excluding Markets, grew 7% year over year, reflecting strength in Services, Wealth and U.S. Consumer Cards. Management expects this metric to increase in the mid-to-high 6% range for 2026, complemented by continued non-interest revenue growth, excluding Markets. Supported by this momentum, management expects 2026 ROTCE to exceed 11%. Citigroup is targeting ROTCE of 11-13% for 2027-2028, with a longer-term objective of achieving sustainable returns of 14-15%. Successful execution of these targets could meaningfully strengthen earnings capacity and improve investor confidence. Hours before the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency published a 47-page report detailing nine banks' missteps with regard to alleged wrongful account closures, the largest of those banks urged a federal court to throw out a lawsuit brought by the debanked-in-chief. Lawyers for JPMorgan Chase argued Tuesday that President Donald Trump's claims against the bank would "fail – multiple times over – and should be dismissed with prejudice." Trump sued JPMorgan and its CEO, Jamie Dimon, in a Florida court in January, accusing the bank of trade libel and breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. Trump also accused Dimon of violating Florida's unfair and deceptive trade practices act by directing JPMorgan to put the plaintiffs on a "blacklist," which allegedly was "published" to other, unnamed banks. JPMorgan's lawyers in February argued the plaintiffs "do not explain what this 'blacklist' entails, when it was created, to whom it was supposedly circulated, or any other detail describing it. "If and when Plaintiffs explain what they mean by this 'blacklist,' JPMorgan will respond accordingly," the bank's lawyers wrote at the time. Now that the case has moved to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, JPMorgan's lawyers are amplifying their stance. "Plaintiffs' allegations regarding the alleged 'blacklist' are so bare that it is impossible to determine what JPMorgan allegedly stated, when, or to whom," the bank's lawyers wrote Tuesday. JPMorgan's lawyers explicitly denied allegations that the bank closed Trump-tied accounts for political reasons or placed them on such a list. One of Trump's personal accounts with JPMorgan remains, the bank argued, adding that several plaintiffs have opened new accounts with JPMorgan. "Moreover, as far as Defendants can tell, no 'blacklist' matching the Complaint's description exists, which is why Plaintiffs cannot identify one," JPMorgan's lawyers wrote. "However, at this stage, the Court need not weigh the veracity of Plaintiffs' allegations, nor accept Plaintiffs' invitation to engage in a policy debate on access to banking. Under well-settled law, even treating Plaintiffs' allegations as true, those allegations fail to state any claim cognizable at law." The bank acknowledged the account agreements the plaintiffs signed "expressly allowed the Bank to close their accounts for any reason (or no reason at all)." "They cannot (and do not) claim any breach of the express terms of those agreements," JPMorgan's lawyers wrote. "Instead, Plaintiffs claim JPMorgan breached an implied contract term, but settled law dictates that an implied contract term may not countermand a contract's express terms." The bank noted, too, that the statute of limitations has run out on both the breach-of-covenant and trade libel claims. Further, the latter "is insufficiently pled," JPMorgan asserted. JPMorgan also argued that Dimon should be excluded from the suit, noting that Trump's claim against him "has already been found legally deficient." title: Specialty lending: The ballast in uncertain markets - J.P. Morgan Private Bank

The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. The superyacht market has no reason to be this steady. Rates have moved sharply, energy prices have swung and the macro backdrop looks meaningfully different from where it was at the start of the year. And yet, order books at the leading shipyards remain full, secondary market pricing has held and the conversations taking place around Monaco, Port Hercules continue as they always do. The question, then, is not whether the yacht market can absorb uncertainty; but rather, are buyers’ financing strategies as equally resilient? The world that owners and buyers are navigating is not the one they anticipated. Rate expectations have swung from cuts to potential hikes, and geopolitical tensions have unsettled energy markets. The first half of 2026 was defined largely by events in the Middle East, which sent energy prices spike higher. In a year of shifting narratives, attention has moved to monetary policy, where the tone has grown more hawkish than most expected. The story the market was telling in January is not the one it is telling now, and has yet to settle. This is not an environment that rewards complacency, and for superyacht owners and prospective buyers, the tension between confidence and caution is likely to shape how capital gets deployed in the months ahead. Complexity has a way of surfacing questions that calmer conditions allow people to defer. Investors will have to consider whether a financing structure has the flexibility to support broader portfolio goals — and if it can hold its shape should conditions shift again. The outlook for the superyacht market remains constructive, and this strength is structural rather than accidental. Order books at the most established shipyards extend years into the future, and that supply constraint has continued to put a floor under secondary market pricing — even as other asset classes have felt the pressure of a more volatile environment. Geopolitical uncertainty and energy price instability have not materially disrupted demand at this level of the market, and the evidence from this year suggests they are unlikely to. For buyers seeking a more immediate path to ownership, the pre-owned market offers a direct and often well-priced route. Alternatively, for those drawn to commissioning their own specifications, new builds remain available on the right timeline. However, the takeaway should be that while conditions are durable, diligent consideration should still be given to the surrounding financial mechanism of any purchase. A thoughtful approach is one that makes ownership more robust and better aligned with the broader portfolio goals that a year like this one tends to bring into focus. When rates fall, clients can capitalise on lower-cost leverage and redeploy capital toward new opportunities. When rates rise, locking in long-term fixed financing on a durable physical asset provides payment certainty and a meaningful buffer against further increases. The structure, if engineered carefully from the outset, performs across both environments rather than becoming a liability when conditions shift. For non-euro clients, currency exposure adds a further dimension that too often enters the conversation late. With the world's leading shipyards concentrated in Europe, recent dollar movements have made hedging a necessary component of any comprehensive financing structure, not a refinement to be addressed once contracts are signed. More broadly, the logic of yacht financing rests on preserving liquidity and maintaining optionality: avoiding the concentration of capital in a single asset and keeping flexibility intact across a broader portfolio. Some clients want a partner to navigate the complexity of a major build alongside them, whereas others are focused on keeping their broader investment architecture intact. A structure designed carefully from the outset serves both, and throughout periods of uncertainty as we have recently seen, that adaptability is paramount. Uncertainty is a reason to structure well, not to wait. Our conversations with clients begin with a single question: What should your wealth accomplish, and how does yacht financing fit within that picture? When that question is answered clearly, the asset supports the plan rather than complicating it. After all, the seas are often rough. The point is to be built to weather the storm. In uncertain markets, specialty lending prices risk by focusing on durability and flexibility: the underlying asset’s resilience (e.g., a durable physical asset), payment certainty through long-term fixed financing when appropriate, and structures that can “hold their shape” if rates or narratives shift again. Lenders navigate changing markets by anticipating shifting narratives (rates, geopolitics, energy) and building adaptable specialty lending structures early — addressing interest-rate strategy up front and, for non-euro clients, integrating currency hedging as a core component rather than a late-stage add-on. The protections that matter most are those that preserve resilience and clarity under volatility: payment certainty (often via long-term fixed-rate structures), disciplined up-front structuring to avoid surprises later, and safeguards that keep broader portfolio flexibility intact rather than concentrating capital in a single asset. Superyacht financing adds market- and execution-specific risks: long timelines for new builds, reliance on shipyard schedules, and — especially for non-euro clients — meaningful currency exposure because leading shipyards are concentrated in Europe, making hedging a necessary part of a comprehensive structure. The superyacht market has held its course for structural reasons: leading shipyards’ order books extend years out, constraining supply and putting a floor under secondary market pricing, while this year’s geopolitical and energy volatility has not materially disrupted demand at the top end. title: Banker-Olympians from J.P. Morgan to Race in Director's Challenge Mixed Eight - Row2k
content: Now in its second year as a major financial sponsor of the Head of the Charles, the J.P. Morgan brand will be increasingly visible up and down the banks of the Charles this weekend. Morgan will be sponsoring the volunteer meals program, the Chase Market Square activity center, the Awards Pavilion, and the Championship Singles Prize, along with co-sponsoring the Director's Tent. Most interestingly, the J.P. Morgan name will also be on several unisuits, as the company will be fielding a boat of nine men and women in the Director's Challenge Mixed Eight, all employed at J.P. Morgan and, remarkably, nearly all Olympians. "The sponsorship isn't just about throwing the name all over the city, which is really cool to see as an employee, but it's also to show that we are serious about the sport, about high performance, and about the kind of community at this regatta," said Jessica Eddie, one of the Olympians in the boat. "We're not just here to have a name on it. We want to actually get involved as a company, in the most literal sense." Eddie works in the asset management team at J.P. Morgan's London office. She is also a two-time Olympian and member of the first-ever British women's eight to win both an Olympic medal (silver) and European championship in 2016. She knew several of her fellow J. P Morgan Olympians from events celebrating Morgan's Olympic sponsorship and its athlete transition program, so when she heard about the Head of the Charles sponsorship earlier this year, she jumped at the chance to put a boat on the water. "I personally badgered the marketing team, and said, 'We've got to get a crew out to actually race! We've just got to!" she said. "Everybody at the bank was super behind it. ... We're so enthusiastic to be here and this race is so special to us, and that's why the minute I mentioned it, everyone jumped to be in the crew." The crew comes not only from different corners of the bank, but also different corners of the world. Artour Samsonov is a Russian-born Harvard alum who raced the coxless pair for Team USA in the 2004 Olympic Games in Athens, and is now based in Luxembourg, where he heads the UK, Ireland, and Luxembourg team for J.P. Morgan's Private Bank. "It's all a bit of a funny story," Samsonov said, calling in from Luxembourg ahead of coming to Boston. "I'm excited to be part of it. I've heard of a few other people in the crew, but I've never met some of them. The reason I haven't met them is because I realized I'm the oldest person in the boat, by far; 2004 is ancient history for a lot of these people in the boat, but rowers tend to attract each other and come together in a funny way because that's the culture of the sport, as we see with this crew." Samsonov was already planning to come for the Regatta-he's racing in a Harvard alumni (Ex-Nemo) boat in the Men's Grand Master Eights on Saturday and visiting family in Massachusetts-so he was happy to jump in the Morgan boat. He said it was the way his company celebrated the spirit of the sport that convinced him. "I've raced with a lot of different people, traveled to a lot of different countries, but the personality type that's attracted to the sport or that's maybe molded by the sport is quite unique and special and when you're around other rowers, you find a lot of common ground, no matter your day job, though the culture at J.P. Morgan is similarly collaborative," he said. "And Head of the Charles means coming full circle back to where elite rowing began for me, and it's a way for me to stay in touch with people. For me, when you come to Head of the Charles, I always say it feels like you died and you went to heaven and all your favorite people are around you." In regard to the phenomenon that is a mixed eight, Samsonov said it was a "cool feeling" to be in a crew of his favorite people, highly accomplished athletes. He remarked that he was proud that the women in the boat, like Irish Olympian Fiona Murtagh, were perhaps the most accomplished. "I love Head of the Charles, it's one of my favorite regattas," said Murtagh, calling in from Cork, Ireland. "I raced the single last year for the first time, which was really fun and really hard-I did not do well around the bends-so when I was told, 'Fiona, you're going to go in an eight, and someone else is going to steer,' I was like, 'Perfect. Sounds like a dream.' "I'm so used to representing my club and my country, but I've never represented my place of work before. That's a really new layer of competing for me, and that's what makes this a really interesting race for me. It's almost combining two really big parts of my life, where now I get to represent where I work in a sport that I love on one of the big stages." Along with working in partner management at J.P. Morgan's Irish office, Murtagh is currently the women's single sculler for Team Ireland. She is a two-time Olympian, winning bronze in the four in Tokyo and racing the pair in Paris. She's won gold and silver in the single in the 2025 and 2026 World Championships, and has her eyes are set on 2028 and Los Angeles. But right now, she's enjoying being a part of the J.P. Morgan crew. "I've never raced the mixed eight, and I'm excited. It's such a great way to keep the sport itself quite new and to make it really fun and really exciting, and it draws new people into the events. It's definitely the kind of event where everyone really enjoys it, and everyone's really intrigued by it," she said. "It's the last event of the Regatta, and one of the most fun to see." Murtagh will be joined by her former pair partner, Aifric Keogh, who will be participating in her first Head of the Charles. Brits Moe Sbihi and James Johnston, Americans Holly Butrico and Brady Leventhal, and German Enno Moench round out the crew, which goes off third in Sunday's last race.

Master trust filings are the monthly window into securitised credit card performance, and a sequential decline in net charge-offs of this size sits within the normal range of month-to-month variation rather than marking a trend break on its own. Historically the card charge-off series has been one of the cleaner real-time reads on the consumer, with deterioration tending to show first in delinquencies before feeding through to charge-offs with a lag of a few months, so the delinquency line in the same filing is the more forward-looking tell. A single month's improvement after a stretch of rising loss rates has, in past cycles, often proved to be noise rather than inflection; the pattern that matters is several consecutive prints moving together across issuers, since idiosyncratic portfolio mix and seasonal factors can move one trust independently of the cohort. For the large card issuers this series is read against the pace of reserve builds and the guidance embedded in card revenue, rather than against the quarter's headline numbers. The follow-ons are the comparable monthly trust filings from the peer card issuers and the next round of delinquency data, which together separate issuer-specific movement from a genuine turn in consumer credit.

title: A unique opportunity to make an impact: Philanthropy after an IPO - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. An IPO can be a defining milestone, often bringing new opportunities alongside increased financial complexity and the need for more intentional planning. For many individuals, it’s also a moment to clarify what they want their wealth to do: support causes and communities they care about, create a legacy, educate and communicate with younger generations, and align resources with long-term priorities. It can be tempting to jump straight into tactics—selecting a structure, selecting a gift amount and choosing organizations. But often, it’s helpful to first step back and view these decisions in the context of your overall vision and values, helping to position your giving strategy for long-term success. To determine if a more structured philanthropic approach makes sense for you, we recommend starting with three key questions outlined below. Philanthropy is personal. Creating a durable plan typically starts by defining what you want your giving to represent—now and over time. This can be a solo exercise, or something you choose to share with a spouse, partner or other trusted stakeholders. These themes will help bring your goals into focus. Your choice of charitable structure—which may vary by jurisdiction—is an important factor in your ability to meet your financial goals, desired involvement, privacy preferences and administrative tolerance. Over time, many philanthropic approaches evolve as needs become more complex and the scope of philanthropic ambition expands. When choosing a vehicle, first clarify your decision-making and operating preferences: If you choose to involve others, a well-defined decision-making process will help ensure that your giving is efficient, consistent and aligned with your objectives. For donors with international interests, it is also important to consider where you are tax resident, where intended recipients are located, whether gifts will cross national borders,  and which reporting and governance requirements apply. Gifts made directly to eligible charitable or nonprofit organizations, as defined under applicable local law.
Benefits: Simplicity; minimal ongoing administration.
Considerations: Less built-in structure for a sustained or multi-year strategy; coordination and recordkeeping can become more complex as giving grows. Where available, a charitable account sponsored by an eligible charitable organization that you fund, and from which you may recommend grants over time.
Benefits: Depending on local law, a DAF or similar structure may allow you to separate the timing of funding from the timing of grantmaking. This approach can be helpful if you want to contribute in a particular year while taking more time to evaluate organizations and define an impact plan. It may also offer administrative simplicity and privacy options.
Considerations: Availability, tax treatment, grant recommendations, investment choices and other features vary by jurisdiction and sponsoring organization. A standalone charitable entity, typically established or supported by a donor and often accompanied by a board and formal governance. Depending on the jurisdiction, trusts, foundations or other vehicles may be tailored to specific philanthropic and planning objectives.
Benefits: Available structures may align charitable goals with timing preferences and broader planning needs, depending on local law and individual circumstances. These often provide the donor with a higher degree of control over charitable strategy and governance.
Considerations: These structures can be complex and may be difficult to change once established; they require careful design and coordination with local legal, tax and other professional advisers. They may involve greater administrative responsibility, recordkeeping, operating costs and formal compliance and governance requirements. Many donors combine approaches—for example, direct gifts for immediate priorities plus a DAF or foundation for longer-term giving. This is often the most practical course of action. As you evaluate options, it helps to assess your current state and cost: how giving is currently managed, which functions are handled directly versus outsourced, whether existing advisors coordinate effectively, whether existing technology meets your needs and the expected startup and ongoing operating costs. It is also important to consider applicable legal, tax, regulatory, reporting and governance requirements in each relevant jurisdiction and to seek appropriate local professional advice. After an IPO, the particular assets you donate, and the timing of those gifts, can matter as much as the vehicle you choose. Some donors prefer to give cash. Others may consider donating securities or more complex assets, depending on their goals and constraints. If planning to donate on a global basis, donors should consider whether and how contributions to a foreign charity are eligible for a charitable deduction in their country of residence. Donors should also consider foreign exchange and currency matters and cross-border reporting and disclosure requirements. Timing can be especially important after an IPO, when income may be elevated and portfolios are being adjusted. Depending on local tax rules and the timing of the sale of shares, donors may consider accelerating or combining planned gifts into a particular tax year, or if spreading gifts over time may be more appropriate. A local tax advisor can help you choose an approach that fits your circumstances. You’ll want to take inventory of your capital and commitments—what you own, the levels of concentration and liquidity, and the priorities that need to be funded. This will help you align your assets with your giving plan, timing preferences and implementation realities. If you plan to donate company shares or other equity interests, you’ll want to coordinate the timing of your donation with the implementation of your broader diversification approach, any applicable transfer restrictions and the legal and tax rules in relevant jurisdictions. Because available structures have different tax attributes and regulatory considerations across jurisdictions, it’s important to approach asset selection deliberately and in coordination with appropriate local legal, tax and other professional advisors. Philanthropic planning is an ongoing process that will evolve alongside your needs, market conditions and long-term objectives. Understanding your motivations, the giving vehicles available to you and the best timing for your gifts are excellent foundations for managing your philanthropic impact. Your J.P. Morgan team can help you navigate the opportunities and complexities of philanthropy and charitable giving following an IPO, and can help you understand your options and resources. title: The art market's second act: beyond the auctions - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Every fall, the art market resets. Fairs open, auction calendars fill and collectors return to the room with fresh eyes and new context. This year, that context is more compelling than usual. The spring auction sales delivered strong double-digit growth, anchored by rare, museum-quality material that had been off the market for years, including works that, in some cases, had not been available in a generation. The results were notable in their own right, yet against a backdrop of global uncertainty, they were remarkable. Whether that momentum carries forward is the question everyone is sitting with. But the auction story is only half of it. Underneath the headline results, a consequential shift is underway in how collectors think about their collections — not just as cultural assets, but as part of a broader financial picture. Specialty lending is at the centre of that shift, and the current market moment has made the conversation more relevant than ever. For collectors, this season raises questions that go beyond the auction room: what could their existing works unlock, and are they positioned to move when something exceptional comes along? Strong auction results have a predictable effect on collectors sitting on significant works. They create a sharpening sense that now might be the moment to act, that the market is receptive and the timing is right. The spring numbers will only intensify that instinct. But selling is a permanent decision in a market that rewards patience, and for many collectors it is simply not an option. Collections carry identity, continuity and narrative across generations. They are not merely financial assets; they are the material record of a family's history and values. No market result, however strong, justifies dismantling that. Specialty lending reframes the question entirely. Rather than asking whether to sell, the more productive conversation is how to access the capital embedded in the collection without giving anything up. Art-secured lending unlocks that liquidity while preserving the collection and the story it tells, keeping the works on the wall while putting capital to work. For collectors who have spent years building something meaningful, that distinction matters. The current market creates the opposite challenge for a different set of collectors: those who want to buy. When rare pieces come to market — and recent lots have demonstrated just how significant they can be — the collectors who act quickly and decisively are the ones who win. That requires liquidity, and liquidity is precisely what many collectors lack when their wealth is concentrated in existing works. Lending against the collection solves that. It frees up capital to pursue new acquisitions without liquidating anything, allowing collectors to move when the opportunity is there rather than watching it pass. The autumn fairs and November sales are exactly the kind of environment where that flexibility matters. In a market defined by selectivity, where the best works attract serious competition and the window to act can be narrow, the ability to move with conviction is itself a strategic advantage. The world that collectors are currently navigating is not the one they anticipated at the start of the year. Rate expectations have swung from cuts to potential hikes, geopolitical uncertainty has unsettled energy markets, and the picture today looks meaningfully different. While the outlook remains constructive, this is not an environment that rewards complacency. Markets have held, and the art market has reflected that resilience in its own way. But for collectors, that tension between confidence and caution is likely to define where and how capital gets deployed. Complexity has a way of surfacing questions that calmer conditions allow collectors to defer. How a collection is structured financially, and whether it has the flexibility to support broader portfolio goals across changing conditions, is one of them. A truly adaptable lending strategy is built for exactly that kind of environment. Our approach to art-secured lending is built around tailored liquidity solutions, designed to deliver stability through any market cycle. An adaptable structure bends and holds, keeping the collection and the broader portfolio intact on the collector's own terms. It is to ensure the collection is working as hard as the rest of your wealth, whatever the environment looks like. The Deloitte Art Market Report projects outstanding art-secured loans reaching $42.0 to $50.1 billion by 2027, reflecting average annual growth of around 11% — a signal that collectors are already thinking differently about what their collections can do.1 The collection should support the plan, not steer it. That means placing it within the full context of your financial picture, objectives, liquidity needs, risk tolerance and time horizon. Our lending structures are built to endure without depending on price appreciation and are focused on significant blue-chip works with comprehensive documentation, credible provenance and transparent market history. What sells in the season ahead will tell us a great deal about where the art market is headed in the long-term. But for collectors, the more important question should whether their collection is working as hard as the rest of their wealth. In a market that remains illiquid outside the very top, access to liquidity is the decisive edge. Specialty lending is no longer an afterthought. For collectors who want to preserve what they have built while staying financially agile, it is how the most thoughtful are staying ahead. Liquidity alternatives like art-secured lending let collectors access capital without selling, while auctions require a permanent decision to part with works. In a market that rewards patience and where collections carry identity and multigenerational narrative, lending can provide liquidity “before the gavel”, while keeping the works and their story intact. The primary alternative described is specialty lending via art-secured lending — borrowing against significant works to unlock liquidity, keep art on the wall, and put capital to work without dismantling a collection. It means having the liquidity and flexibility to move quickly and decisively when rare, museum-quality material comes to market — so you can pursue new acquisitions in competitive fall fairs and November sales without liquidating existing works. Plan for shifting macro conditions that can change quickly — rate expectations moving from cuts to potential hikes, geopolitical uncertainty affecting energy markets and broader volatility that can influence how and when you deploy capital. The key risk is being structurally unprepared: lacking a financing setup that can support broader portfolio goals across changing conditions. A portfolio-first approach places the collection inside the full context of your wealth plan — objectives, liquidity needs, risk tolerance and time horizon — so the collection supports the plan rather than steering it. Lending is structured to endure without relying on price appreciation, typically focused on significant blue-chip works with strong documentation, credible provenance, and transparent market history. CEO Jamie Dimon cited the firm's ability to grow its customer base and maintain its leadership in retail deposit share, stating, "We retained our number 1 position in retail deposit share based on FDIC data." Looking forward, management highlighted a constructive but uncertain outlook, with a focus on navigating a dynamic macroeconomic environment and ongoing investment in technology and risk management. Management attributed the quarter's performance to resilient consumer and business banking, continued investment, and strong asset management flows, but cited higher expenses and some market-related headwinds. Net interest income trends: Management's guidance for net interest income (NII) relies on moderate consumer and wholesale deposit growth, a stable yield curve, and ongoing loan demand. Credit and consumer health: The resilience of consumer credit quality and stable corporate credit outlook are central to future performance. Savers are exposing themselves to major financial risks by allowing AI bots to manage their money, the boss of JP Morgan has warned. Jamie Dimon, the Wall Street chief executive, said the growing use of autonomous agents to help people with their finances was a problem if the bots got things wrong. Mr Dimon said customers could end up being liable for mistakes made by any agent acting on their behalf. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," he said. "We have to make sure we protect our customers in the right kind of way. "We will be building tools to do that too. In the meantime, we're not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside the company because that's just too risky for clients and for JP Morgan." The warning from Wall Street puts it into direct conflict with Silicon Valley, which has pushed AI bots as a way to help people with their finances. OpenAI's ChatGPT announced a "personal finance experience" for the chatbot's paid users in the US several months ago. The tool allows customers to securely connect their financial accounts, see a dashboard of where their money is going and ask ChatGPT questions based on their own finances. Anthropic is also reportedly testing a similar feature, called Claude Money. More than half of consumers in the UK already use AI tools and a quarter use the technology for financial tasks at least once a month, according to a survey by McKinsey. That figure rises to 59pc among high-income consumers. There are also increasing concerns that AI could lead to a rapid run on a bank, as agents make it even easier to move cash from one bank to another. The technology could also hit banks' profits as AI bots move customers' cash out of zero-interest current accounts in search of better returns. Savers could shift up to £700bn out of accounts that offer little or no returns and into savings products on the advice of AI chatbots in the UK, according to consultants at McKinsey. If just 5pc to 10pc of bank balances are moved this way, the profits lenders make on deposits could drop by a fifth or more. Mr Dimon said that in the future banks would adjust to new ways of making money, perhaps through subscriptions or other services. However, he added that there was more risk in the short term, as AI agents are let loose on the financial sector. "Should regulators be thinking about what they're going to do with some of these things? Yeah, of course they should," Mr Dimon said. "It's a new world and with all these bots and agents, could someone ... cause a problem? Maybe." The warning came as JP Morgan reported a rare miss on profit in the third quarter of the year, as its bond trading revenue dropped by 4pc year-on-year. Total trading revenue was $10.3bn for the period, below Wall Street expectations of $10.5bn. Goldman Sachs also saw a small 1pc drop in bond trading to $3.47bn, significantly lower than expected. title: JPMorgan Chase blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from directly accessing accounts - CNBC
content:
JPMorgan Chase won’t allow outside artificial intelligence agents to access customer accounts and operate on their behalf, CEO Jamie Dimon said Tuesday, citing risks to the company and its customers as tech firms including Meta release autonomous assistants. “We’re not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company, because it’s just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan,” Dimon told analysts on the bank’s third-quarter earnings call. “You don’t want rogue agents, and it could be thousands of them,” he added, describing the potential threat to customers. In July, an OpenAI model hacked into AI company Hugging Face’s servers. The stance from Dimon, the longtime CEO of the biggest U.S. bank by assets and a de facto spokesman for the U.S. financial sector, is reminiscent of an earlier fight with fintech firms over access to customer data. JPMorgan moved to charge data middlemen including Plaid for access, a dispute that similarly pitted the bank’s security concerns against tech firms’ demands for access. A JPMorgan spokeswoman confirmed to CNBC that the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers. “Protecting our customers is our top priority. Because it is not safe, we do not permit third parties to access accounts by obtaining customers’ banking credentials and logging in on their behalf,” the spokeswoman said. “We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers and are committed to enabling agentic connections securely,” she added. That means that AI agents can access some customer data from Chase accounts in a read-only fashion, such as customer balances, if Plaid or another connector has the user’s credentials. But they can’t send money or pay a bill — actions that make an agent useful. There’s no timeline for when the bank would have safeguards in place to allow agents to directly interact with customer accounts, the spokeswoman added. Dimon said JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them for customer-facing applications. The bank’s approach, he said, isn’t about being for or against the technology, but about ensuring it serves customers safely. In recent weeks, JPMorgan began a targeted pilot for its own AI tool called Smart Cash, which aims to predict a user’s cash flow and move funds to maximize yield, Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. That would appear to be a defensive move against external agents. Dimon also seemed to draw a line about liability when customers authorize outside AI agents to act on their behalf. “If people are using them, they should understand the risk,” Dimon said. “They should understand there’s a liability transfer.” Personal agents have gained mainstream popularity in recent months as AI models integrate more autonomy, like the ability to cancel subscriptions or use credit cards on a user’s behalf, for example. Instinct, a digital concierge that relies primarily on text messaging instead of an app, launched earlier this year on an invitation-only basis. The startup behind the service, San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, was founded last year and reached a $10 billion valuation last month. In September, bank stocks were hit as Meta’s Muse agent topped the app download charts shortly after it was unveiled, sparking fears that consumers would use agents to move funds from low-yielding accounts to higher-yielding ones. Weeks later, OpenAI released its own agent, Dots. Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok and others pointed to the risks that agents pose to cheap bank deposits. But that risk will be limited if agents aren’t allowed to operate freely with customers’ accounts. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you.
